steps.lessonTitle: Pick your training route
steps.title: Create your evidence folder
steps.where: Physical Windows host / File Explorer / lab notes; no Azure deployment.
steps.action: On the physical host, open File Explorer and create a SONIC-Lab folder with subfolders Installers, Screenshots, Baselines, and Backups. Keep passwords elsewhere.
steps.expected: The four folders exist on storage with sufficient free space.

steps.lessonTitle: Pick your training route
steps.title: Record the version journey
steps.where: Physical Windows host / File Explorer / lab notes; no Azure deployment.
steps.action: Create a lab note: VMware Workstation Pro on the host; Windows Server 2019 Desktop Experience on premises; Server 2019 Azure destination; migrate test workload/data; then upgrade that Azure member server to Server 2022.
steps.expected: Your note distinguishes moving an application from moving a whole VM.

steps.lessonTitle: Pick your training route
steps.title: Choose the required route
steps.where: Physical Windows host / File Explorer / lab notes; no Azure deployment.
steps.action: Complete the Windows/AD core, SQL core, Azure foundations, and migration core in sidebar order. Leave MECM and high availability extensions until their prerequisites pass.
steps.expected: DC01/DC02 and APP01 are prepared before the migration work.

steps.lessonTitle: Understand the map
steps.title: Record the named outcome
steps.where: Physical Windows host / lab worksheet; read-only planning.
steps.action: # Understand the map
steps.expected: Compare your recorded result with the named lesson evidence before marking verified.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Confirm Workstation Pro
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro / official ISO download; authorized local administrator for installation.
steps.action: On your physical Windows PC, open VMware Workstation Pro > Help > About. Record the installed version. This course uses Workstation, not vCenter or ESXi.
steps.expected: The product is Workstation Pro and it can create Windows Server 2019 guests.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Obtain Server 2019 media
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro / official ISO download; authorized local administrator for installation.
steps.action: Use the Windows Server 2019 ISO your course or license administrator supplies. For local-only evaluation, open https://www.microsoft.com/evalcenter/evaluate-windows-server-2019 and download the 64-bit ISO. Save it under Installers.
steps.expected: The media is Windows Server 2019, not 2025.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Choose the media and license path
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro / official ISO download; authorized local administrator for installation.
steps.action: Record language, edition, evaluation/licensed status, and whether Desktop Experience is available. The Azure upgrade exercise uses a licensed/pay-as-you-go 2019 Marketplace member VM with a matching 2022 upgrade path.
steps.expected: Your source and destination license choices are written down.

steps.lessonTitle: Prepare your laptop and downloads
steps.title: Check host resources
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro / official ISO download; authorized local administrator for installation.
steps.action: On the host press Ctrl+Shift+Esc > Performance. Record available RAM and disk space. Plan roughly 4 GB RAM per DC and APP01, with more for SQL; run optional servers only when the host can accommodate them.
steps.expected: The host has enough free resources for the next required pair of VMs.

steps.lessonTitle: Build one safe VMware network
steps.title: Open the network editor
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro Virtual Network Editor; authorized host administrator.
steps.action: On the physical host open Workstation Pro > Edit > Virtual Network Editor. Click Change Settings if shown and approve the local Windows administrator prompt.
steps.expected: You can edit virtual-network settings.

steps.lessonTitle: Build one safe VMware network
steps.title: Create a dedicated NAT VMnet
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro Virtual Network Editor; authorized host administrator.
steps.action: Click Add Network. Choose an unused VMnet, for example VMnet2. Select NAT. Do not edit the VMnet used by unrelated VMs.
steps.expected: A dedicated NAT network appears in the list.

steps.lessonTitle: Build one safe VMware network
steps.title: Set a non-overlapping subnet
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro Virtual Network Editor; authorized host administrator.
steps.action: For the example plan set Subnet IP to 192.168.77.0 and Subnet mask to 255.255.255.0 only after checking it does not overlap your host, home router, VPN, or Azure address range.
steps.expected: Your chosen lab subnet is private and does not overlap another route you use.

steps.lessonTitle: Build one safe VMware network
steps.title: Record the actual NAT gateway
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro Virtual Network Editor; authorized host administrator.
steps.action: Click NAT Settings. Read the Gateway IP and write it down exactly, then close the dialog. Do not assume it ends in .1 or .2.
steps.expected: Your worksheet has VMnet name, subnet, mask, and gateway.

steps.lessonTitle: Build one safe VMware network
steps.title: Reserve the static lab addresses
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro Virtual Network Editor; authorized host administrator.
steps.action: Open DHCP Settings and reserve a static range outside its lease pool, or disable VMware DHCP for this dedicated static-only lab. Plan .10 AG-DC01, .11 AG-DC02, .20 APP01, .60 SQL01, and .70 MECM01 within the chosen /24. Apply and close.
steps.expected: No static server address overlaps a DHCP lease or another server.

steps.lessonTitle: Build one safe VMware network
steps.title: Attach each guest to this VMnet
steps.where: Physical Windows host / Workstation Pro Virtual Network Editor; authorized host administrator.
steps.action: With a lab VM powered off, right-click it > Settings > Network Adapter. Choose Custom and your recorded VMnet. Enable Connect at power on.
steps.expected: All on-prem lab servers use the same dedicated VMnet.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Open the new VM wizard
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: On your physical Windows PC, open VMware Workstation Pro. Click File, then New Virtual Machine. Do not do this inside another VM.
steps.expected: The New Virtual Machine Wizard is open.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose Typical
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Select Typical (recommended), then Next. The reference image has Custom selected; use the upper Typical radio button for this lab.
steps.expected: The wizard asks how the guest operating system will be installed.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Use manual Windows installation
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Select I will install the operating system later, then Next. This avoids Easy Install silently choosing an edition.
steps.expected: The wizard lets you choose a guest OS profile.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose the Server 2019 guest profile
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Select Microsoft Windows. Open Version and choose Windows Server 2019, then Next.
steps.expected: The guest profile says Windows Server 2019.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Name the VM
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Enter AG-DC01 as the virtual machine name. Browse to a folder with enough free space, such as your dedicated SONIC lab folder, then Next.
steps.expected: The summary uses AG-DC01 and a location you can find again.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Create a new virtual disk
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Set Maximum disk size to 60 GB for this lab plan. Choose Split virtual disk into multiple files, then Next. Do not attach an existing production disk.
steps.expected: A new blank virtual disk is selected.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Set memory and CPU
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Click Customize Hardware. Select Memory and enter 4096 MB. Select Processors and use 1 processor with 2 cores for the basic lab.
steps.expected: The hardware list shows your memory allocation and two virtual cores.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Attach the Server 2019 ISO
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Select CD/DVD in the hardware list. Choose Use ISO image file, Browse to your Windows Server 2019 ISO, and enable Connect at power on.
steps.expected: The CD/DVD path ends with your Server 2019 ISO filename.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Attach the private VMnet
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Select Network Adapter. Choose Custom: Specific virtual network and the NAT VMnet recorded in LAB 03. Enable Connected and Connect at power on.
steps.expected: The VM is attached to the same private lab VMnet as the other lab servers.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Finish and start the VM
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Click Close, then Finish. Select the new VM in the Workstation library and click Power on this virtual machine. Click inside its console and press a key when the ISO boot prompt appears.
steps.expected: Windows Setup appears inside the VM console.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Start Windows Setup
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Choose the language you need for the course, time format, and keyboard, then Next and Install now. Use English (United States) media if you will follow the Azure upgrade-media route later.
steps.expected: Setup displays an edition list or asks for a legitimate product key.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose Desktop Experience
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Select Windows Server 2019 Standard (Desktop Experience), or the matching authorized Datacenter (Desktop Experience) edition your course supplies. If using Evaluation for local practice, record that limitation. Click Next and accept the license only if you agree.
steps.expected: The selected line explicitly includes 2019 and Desktop Experience.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Install only on the new blank disk
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Choose Custom: Install Windows only (advanced). Select the new VM’s blank Drive 0 unallocated space and click Next. This is a clean install in a new VM, not the later Azure in-place upgrade.
steps.expected: Windows copies files, installs, and restarts.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Create the local Administrator password
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: At Customize settings, set and confirm a strong local Administrator password. Save it in your own password manager, then Finish.
steps.expected: The Windows sign-in screen appears.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Sign into the guest
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Use Workstation VM > Send Ctrl+Alt+Del (or Ctrl+Alt+Insert), then sign in as the guest’s local Administrator.
steps.expected: You see a Windows desktop and Server Manager.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Install VMware Tools
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: In Workstation select VM > Install VMware Tools. In the guest open File Explorer > This PC, open the VMware Tools CD, and run setup64.exe if offered. Choose the normal setup and restart when asked.
steps.expected: After restart, the guest is usable with the expected mouse/display integration.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Patch the new Server 2019 guest
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Inside the guest open Start > Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update. Check for updates and restart as required before changing its DNS to the new lab domain.
steps.expected: Windows has completed its pending restarts.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Rename Windows
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Inside the guest press Win+R, enter sysdm.cpl, and press Enter. On Computer Name choose Change. Enter AG-DC01, confirm OK, and restart when prompted.
steps.expected: After signing in again, hostname returns AG-DC01.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Open the guest IPv4 settings
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Inside the guest press Win+R, type ncpa.cpl, and press Enter. Right-click the connected Ethernet adapter > Properties. Select Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4), then Properties.
steps.expected: The IPv4 address and DNS fields are visible.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Enter the lab address
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: For the example LAB 03 network only, choose Use the following IP address: 192.168.77.10; subnet mask 255.255.255.0; gateway = the NAT gateway you recorded in LAB 03. Set preferred DNS to 192.168.77.10. Click OK and Close. If you changed the subnet in LAB 03, use your matching address plan instead.
steps.expected: ipconfig /all shows the chosen private address, gateway, and DNS on the connected adapter.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Confirm this is Server 2019
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Open Start, search Windows PowerShell, right-click it > Run as administrator. Run the read-only inventory below in this VM.
steps.command:
hostname
Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber
DISM /online /Get-CurrentEdition
steps.expected: WindowsProductName identifies Windows Server 2019; hostname identifies AG-DC01.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Open Add Roles and Features
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Inside the named server open Server Manager. Choose Manage > Add Roles and Features. Click Next on Before you begin.
steps.expected: The Select installation type page is shown.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Select the local destination server
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Choose Role-based or feature-based installation > Next. Select a server from the server pool and select this VM’s computer name > Next.
steps.expected: The Server Roles page targets the correct computer.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Select AD DS and its tools
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Check Active Directory Domain Services. In the pop-up click Add Features, then Next.
steps.expected: AD DS is selected and its required management tools are included.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Install the role
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Keep the required Features selected. Click Next through the AD DS information page, review the selected target, then click Install.
steps.expected: Installation succeeds and offers Promote this server to a domain controller.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Choose the correct promotion operation
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Click Promote this server to a domain controller. Choose Add a new forest. Enter cloudseam.tech as Root domain name. Click Next.
steps.expected: The wizard shows a NEW forest named cloudseam.tech.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Set controller options and DSRM
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: For Server 2019 in this lab, use Windows Server 2016 for both forest and domain functional levels. Keep DNS server and Global Catalog selected. Set and confirm a unique DSRM recovery password, store it securely, then Next.
steps.expected: Required options are selected and the password boxes have no validation error.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Review DNS and additional options
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Continue past the isolated-root DNS-delegation warning only if it is the expected warning for this private lab. Confirm the CLOUDSEAM NetBIOS name on Additional Options.
steps.expected: The wizard advances without a blocking validation error.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Keep the default AD paths
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: On Paths keep the default NTDS database/log and SYSVOL locations for this small lab, then Next.
steps.expected: The wizard shows Review Options.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Check prerequisites before promotion
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: On Review Options confirm cloudseam.tech, the correct computer, and DNS. Click Next, then wait for Prerequisites Check.
steps.expected: The prerequisite check succeeds; only understood lab warnings remain.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Promote and wait for restart
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Click Install only after the prerequisite check passes. Wait for the VM to restart; do not power it off to shorten the wait.
steps.expected: The guest restarts and offers a domain sign-in.

steps.lessonTitle: Make AG-DC01: the agency begins
steps.title: Verify the directory
steps.where: Physical host Workstation Pro, then AG-DC01 guest / Server 2019 Desktop Experience / local Administrator, then CLOUDSEAM domain Administrator.
steps.action: Sign in with your authorized cloudseam.tech administrator account. Open Windows PowerShell as administrator in this VM and run the checks.
steps.command:
hostname
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName
Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.cloudseam.tech
steps.expected: The DNSRoot is cloudseam.tech and domain-controller records resolve to the lab’s private IPs.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Open Active Directory Users and Computers
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: Inside AG-DC01 open Server Manager > Tools > Active Directory Users and Computers. Expand cloudseam.tech in the left pane.
steps.expected: You are managing the cloudseam.tech directory on AG-DC01.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Create the Operations OU
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: Right-click cloudseam.tech > New > Organizational Unit. Enter Operations. Leave protection from accidental deletion enabled, then OK. Repeat to create Security.
steps.expected: Both OUs appear under cloudseam.tech.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Create the test user
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: Right-click Operations > New > User. Enter a fictional name and user logon name test.analyst. Click Next, set a private temporary password, choose your lab password-change requirement, Next, then Finish.
steps.expected: test.analyst appears in Operations.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Create and populate the group
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: Right-click Operations > New > Group. Name it GG-Operations, select Global and Security, then OK. Open the group > Members > Add; enter test.analyst > Check Names > OK.
steps.expected: Members lists the new test user.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Open Group Policy Management
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: In Server Manager choose Tools > Group Policy Management. Expand Forest: cloudseam.tech > Domains > cloudseam.tech.
steps.expected: The Operations OU appears in the policy tree.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Create and link the GPO
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: Right-click Operations > Create a GPO in this domain, and Link it here. Name it LAB-Operations-Banner and click OK.
steps.expected: The named GPO is linked under Operations.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Edit the logon banner
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: Right-click the linked GPO > Edit. Expand Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. Set the interactive logon message title to CLOUDSEAM LAB and message text to This is a practice environment.
steps.expected: The two banner settings show your lab text.

steps.lessonTitle: Create test users, OUs, and a GPO
steps.title: Verify the objects
steps.where: AG-DC01 guest / Server Manager, ADUC, and GPMC / authorized cloudseam.tech administrator.
steps.action: On AG-DC01 run these read-only checks and capture ADUC plus the GPO link.
steps.expected: The user, group membership, and GPO are returned.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection
steps.title: Start on your own Windows computer
steps.where: Your Windows computer at home · web browser
steps.action:
Use the Windows computer you will use to connect to the lab. Open your browser and go to https://portal.azure.com. Sign in with the Azure account used in the earlier lessons.
You will create the rule by clicking in the Azure website. PowerShell will only help you write down one value. You do not need Azure Cloud Shell, an administrator PowerShell window, or a connection to RHEL for this lesson.
An NSG, short for Network Security Group, is a list of network traffic rules. Inbound means coming into the Azure VM. Outbound means leaving it. Your connection leaves your Windows computer and arrives at the VM, so the VM needs an INBOUND rule.
SSH is the secure connection you will use to type commands on Linux from Windows. Port 22 is the numbered connection point SSH normally uses. This rule lets your home connection reach that point. You still need the correct username and SSH key to sign in.
steps.expected: The Azure website is open on your own Windows computer. You know why this is an inbound rule.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection
steps.title: Create the empty list of network rules
steps.where: Your Windows computer · Azure website
steps.action:
Click the search box at the top of the Azure page. Type Network security groups. Click Network security groups in the results. Click Create.
For Subscription, select the subscription recorded earlier. For Resource group, select rg-rhel9-lab. For Name, type nsg-rhel9-lab. For Region, choose the same region as your lab network.
Click Review + create. Read the names once more. Click Create. Wait for the completion message, then click Go to resource. If that button is missing, search Network security groups again and click nsg-rhel9-lab.
If nsg-rhel9-lab already exists from your earlier work, open it and inspect it instead of creating another one.
steps.expected: The page for nsg-rhel9-lab is open. You have not connected it to a VM yet.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection
steps.title: Find the public address of your home connection
steps.where: Your Windows computer · Azure website · nsg-rhel9-lab
steps.action:
On the left of the NSG page, click Inbound security rules. Click Add. In Source, select My IP address. Read the address Azure fills in. Write down the IPv4 address: four groups of numbers separated by dots. Do not click Add yet.
This public address is what Azure sees when your computer connects over the internet. It is usually the address of your home router’s internet connection. It is not the private address shown by ipconfig, and it is not the Azure VM’s address.
If you are using a VPN or browser proxy, the browser and SSH may use different public addresses. Use the approved network instructions to confirm the address SSH will use. Do not guess or turn off a required workplace VPN.
Add /32 after the address. Here /32 means “this one IPv4 address.” If Azure already included /32, keep it once. Do not use the example address from another lesson.
steps.expected: You have your current public IPv4 followed by /32. The new rule is still unsaved.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection
steps.title: Open PowerShell on your Windows computer and save that value
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Click Windows Start. Type Windows Terminal and open it. Click the small down arrow next to the + tab button, then choose Windows PowerShell or PowerShell. If Windows Terminal is not installed, click Start, type Windows PowerShell, and open that app normally.
Look for a prompt beginning with PS and a Windows folder, such as PS C:\Users\YourName>. You are on your own computer. Do not type these lines at a Linux prompt, at sftp>, or in Azure Cloud Shell.
Run the first line below and press Enter. PowerShell asks you to type your public IPv4 followed by /32. Type the value you just wrote down and press Enter. Then run the second line.
$AdminSourceCidr is a named box in PowerShell memory. Read-Host asks you for text and puts your answer in that box. The second line displays it so you can check it. These lines do not create a rule or change Azure. If you close this tab, the value is forgotten; your written notes are the lasting record.
steps.command:
$AdminSourceCidr = Read-Host "Type your current public IPv4 followed by /32"
$AdminSourceCidr
steps.expected: PowerShell prints the exact address you entered, ending in /32. Check it against Azure before continuing.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection
steps.title: Fill in who can connect
steps.where: Your Windows computer · return to the Azure Add inbound security rule form
steps.action:
Set Source to IP Addresses. In Source IP addresses/CIDR ranges, enter the public IPv4/32 you just checked. “Source” means where the connection starts. CIDR is Azure’s name for the address format with /32.
Set Source port ranges to *. Windows chooses a temporary outgoing port for each connection, so leave this field as *. This does not allow every source IP address; the address field above still restricts who can connect.
Set Destination to Any. This means the destination covered by this NSG when you attach it to the intended VM network card later. Keep this NSG for that lab VM. Set Service to Custom.
steps.expected: The source address is your current public IPv4/32. Source port is *. Destination is Any. Service is Custom.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection
steps.title: Fill in what connection is allowed and save
steps.where: Your Windows computer · same Azure rule form
steps.action:
In Destination port ranges, type 22. Set Protocol to TCP. TCP is the type of network connection SSH uses. Set Action to Allow.
Set Priority to 300. Azure checks lower numbers first. If 300 is already used, inspect the existing rule before choosing an unused number and record your choice. Do not overwrite an unrelated rule.
In Name, type Allow-SSH-rexuser-workstation. Read each field again, then click Add. Wait for the new rule to appear in Inbound security rules.
Do not add an outbound rule in this step. Do not add Wazuh ports yet. Keep the Azure default rules; this lesson adds one rule for SSH from your public address.
steps.expected: The new inbound rule is listed with your source /32, destination port 22, TCP and Allow.

steps.lessonTitle: Allow SSH from your home connection

steps.where: Your Windows computer · Azure website and your lab notes
steps.action:
Click the rule you created and compare its fields with the previous steps. Check that no other custom rule allows SSH from Any or 0.0.0.0/0. Those values could allow connections from anywhere on the internet.
Write down the NSG name, rule name, source address, port and priority. The NSG is not attached yet; the VM creation lesson will select it for the VM network card, also called a NIC. Later, repeat these steps for the manager’s separate NSG.
If your home public IP changes later, sign in to Azure, open this NSG → Inbound security rules → this rule. Record the old value, change only the source to your new verified IPv4/32, and click Save. Test SSH again. Do not change the source to Any to make a connection work.
If a later edit breaks access, compare it with your saved notes and restore the last correct specific value. Keep Azure website access available while testing. Do not delete the whole NSG to fix one rule.
steps.expected: Your notes match the saved rule. You understand that a successful rule creation is not yet a successful SSH login.

steps.title: Generate the pair only after both checks say False
steps.where: Your Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user

At Enter passphrase, type a strong passphrase and press Enter. Type it again when asked. You may see no characters while typing; that is normal. Keep it in your approved password manager.
If asked whether to overwrite a file, type n and press Enter, then stop. That means the previous file check needs to be repeated.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Read the error before choosing a fix
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE, permissions are too open, or Load key: bad permissions means Windows SSH rejected the local private-key file. Use the key-permission steps below for that error.
Connection timed out means start with the VM power state, correct IP, inbound TCP 22 rule and network route. Connection refused usually means the destination was reached but no service accepted the port, or a device actively rejected it. Changing key permissions will not fix those problems.
Permission denied (publickey) by itself has several possible causes: wrong account, wrong key, missing authorized public key, server permissions or server policy. Check the actual VM build record. Do not guess another username or open SSH to everyone.
A host fingerprint prompt is a separate check. Compare it with the fingerprint obtained through the earlier Azure Run Command lesson before accepting. A changed or unfamiliar fingerprint is not permission to type yes automatically.
steps.expected: You have identified the exact error and chosen the matching troubleshooting branch.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Find your Windows account, computer name and exact key file
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Run whoami to see the signed-in Windows account. $env:COMPUTERNAME shows the computer’s name, not the processor model. Windows uses a SID, a stable account number, to identify the account even if its display name changes.
At the path prompt, enter the full path to the private key you already use. Do not include extra quote characters in the answer. The commands quote the variable for you, so spaces in a folder name are handled.
The private key may end in .pem or have no extension. Do not select its .pub partner. Never paste the key’s contents into the course or a support ticket.
steps.command:
whoami
$env:COMPUTERNAME
$SonicUserSid = [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().User.Value
$SonicUserSid
$SonicKey = Read-Host "Full path to your existing private key"
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $SonicKey -PathType Leaf)) { throw "File not found: stop" }
$SonicKey = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Path
steps.expected: The Windows account and key path are correct. No permission has changed.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Inspect the owner and who can read the key
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
icacls lists the file’s permission entries. R means read, W means write, M means modify, F means full control, and I means inherited from the parent folder. Inheritance means a file receives permissions from its folder.
Get-Acl shows the owner and a table of entries. Allow gives access; Deny blocks access. Check the file itself and its parent folder. Removing inheritance does not remove permissions that were added directly to the file.
For your personal client key, use your own account as owner and restrict access to that account under workplace policy. Reading is enough for SSH to use it. Other ordinary users or shared groups should not read it. Do not copy Windows SSH server authorized_keys permission recipes onto this personal private key.
If the owner is another account, the file is centrally managed, or access is denied, stop and ask the Windows administrator to repair this exact file. Do not take ownership of a folder tree. If elevation is required, reopen PowerShell with Run as administrator under the intended identity and recheck whoami first.
Keep keys under %USERPROFILE%\.ssh, outside OneDrive and the repository. If this key is in a synced/shared folder, arrange a move to that local folder while preserving working access. After moving it, repeat the path-selection and inspection cards with its new path before continuing. Moving it does not erase older shared or cloud copies; replace an exposed key through your normal key-rotation process.
steps.command:
icacls "$SonicKey"
$SonicKeyFolder = [System.IO.Path]::GetDirectoryName($SonicKey)
icacls "$SonicKeyFolder"
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Owner
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Access | Select-Object IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited
steps.expected: You know the owner, your account SID and the exact unwanted entries before changing anything.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Save the current permissions before editing
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
This saves permission information, not the private-key contents. Keep the backup path in your local notes. /save saves the file’s access list; it is not a backup of the key and does not save its owner.
Push-Location temporarily opens the key’s parent folder so the saved filename can be restored to the same folder later. Pop-Location returns to your previous folder.
If saving fails, stop. Do not continue with an unknown recovery path.
steps.command:
$SonicAclFolder = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA "SONIC"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $SonicAclFolder -Force | Out-Null
$SonicAclBackup = Join-Path $SonicAclFolder ("key-acl-" + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString() + ".txt")
$SonicKeyName = [System.IO.Path]::GetFileName($SonicKey)
Push-Location -LiteralPath $SonicKeyFolder
icacls "$SonicKeyName" /save "$SonicAclBackup"
$SonicAclSaved = $LASTEXITCODE
Pop-Location
if ($SonicAclSaved -ne 0) { throw "ACL backup failed: stop" }
$SonicAclBackup
steps.expected: The permission backup was saved successfully and its path is recorded.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Give your own account read access, then remove inherited entries
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Use this only for the personally owned key checked above. Run one line at a time. /grant:r replaces the explicit Allow entry for this SID only. It does not remove other users, groups or Deny entries.
The * tells icacls that the value is a numeric SID. R gives read access. Adding your explicit entry first avoids removing your only inherited access.
/inheritance:r turns off inheritance and removes inherited entries from this file. It does not touch every file in the folder. Stop on any error.
steps.expected: Your explicit read entry exists. Review any remaining explicit entries in the next step.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Remove only a confirmed unwanted explicit entry
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
If the permission list still shows an unwanted account or group, copy its exact SID from the error or identify it with the Windows administrator. Do not enter your own SID. Do not remove entries from a whole folder tree.
S-1-5-32 identifies the Windows BUILTIN domain; it is not a universal name for every built-in group. Use the exact offending entry shown for your file. Do not copy another person’s account SID from a screenshot.
The command below removes entries for the chosen SID only. Run it once per reviewed unwanted entry, then inspect the list again. If the remaining entries are unclear or policy-managed, use the administrator rather than guessing.
GUI alternative: File Explorer → the exact key → right-click → Properties → Security → Advanced. Check Owner. Select only an unwanted permission entry → Remove. Keep your account’s Read entry → Apply → OK. Inspect again. Do not reset the whole folder.
Do not use /reset as the normal fix: it replaces the file’s permissions with inherited defaults and can make the key readable by others again.
steps.expected: Only the intended personal-key access remains. No shared group or unrelated user can read the key.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: Try SSH again with the recorded Linux username
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Enter the VM’s current public IP and the Linux username from its creation record. This course uses rexuser. If your own VM was created with a different name, use the verified name—not a guess based on the error.
Keep the path in quotes. -i selects this private key; IdentitiesOnly=yes prevents SSH from trying unrelated keys. Verify any host fingerprint against trusted notes. A passphrase prompt unlocks the local key; it is not an Azure password prompt.
If the too-open warning is gone but Permission denied remains, the local file fix worked and another check is needed. Verify the selected public key was installed for the recorded Linux account, then inspect that account’s server-side SSH settings through the approved recovery route. Do not disable host checking or switch usernames blindly.
steps.command:
$SonicVmAddress = Read-Host "VM public IP from Azure"
$SonicVmUser = Read-Host "Linux username from the VM build record"
ssh -i "$SonicKey" -o IdentitiesOnly=yes "$SonicVmUser@$SonicVmAddress"
steps.expected: The local key warning is gone. A successful Linux login is verified separately with whoami and hostname.

steps.lessonTitle: Create and inspect the rexuser key pair
steps.title: If a permission edit goes wrong, restore the saved access list
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
This is a recovery branch, not a routine step after a successful repair. Use the exact same parent folder and saved ACL file. If you reopened PowerShell, enter their recorded paths again first.
Restoring the old access list may also restore the original too-open problem. It returns you to the saved state so you can diagnose safely; it does not promise SSH will work. It does not restore an owner change.
If you can no longer read or manage the file, ask the Windows administrator to restore the saved access list for this exact file. Do not reset permissions recursively on your profile or .ssh directory.
steps.expected: The saved access list is restored, or the exact restore error is recorded for the administrator.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Read the error before choosing a fix
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE, permissions are too open, or Load key: bad permissions means Windows SSH rejected the local private-key file. Use the key-permission steps below for that error.
Connection timed out means start with the VM power state, correct IP, inbound TCP 22 rule and network route. Connection refused usually means the destination was reached but no service accepted the port, or a device actively rejected it. Changing key permissions will not fix those problems.
Permission denied (publickey) by itself has several possible causes: wrong account, wrong key, missing authorized public key, server permissions or server policy. Check the actual VM build record. Do not guess another username or open SSH to everyone.
A host fingerprint prompt is a separate check. Compare it with the fingerprint obtained through the earlier Azure Run Command lesson before accepting. A changed or unfamiliar fingerprint is not permission to type yes automatically.
steps.expected: You have identified the exact error and chosen the matching troubleshooting branch.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Find your Windows account, computer name and exact key file
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Run whoami to see the signed-in Windows account. $env:COMPUTERNAME shows the computer’s name, not the processor model. Windows uses a SID, a stable account number, to identify the account even if its display name changes.
At the path prompt, enter the full path to the private key you already use. Do not include extra quote characters in the answer. The commands quote the variable for you, so spaces in a folder name are handled.
The private key may end in .pem or have no extension. Do not select its .pub partner. Never paste the key’s contents into the course or a support ticket.
steps.command:
whoami
$env:COMPUTERNAME
$SonicUserSid = [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().User.Value
$SonicUserSid
$SonicKey = Read-Host "Full path to your existing private key"
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $SonicKey -PathType Leaf)) { throw "File not found: stop" }
$SonicKey = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Path
steps.expected: The Windows account and key path are correct. No permission has changed.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Inspect the owner and who can read the key
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
icacls lists the file’s permission entries. R means read, W means write, M means modify, F means full control, and I means inherited from the parent folder. Inheritance means a file receives permissions from its folder.
Get-Acl shows the owner and a table of entries. Allow gives access; Deny blocks access. Check the file itself and its parent folder. Removing inheritance does not remove permissions that were added directly to the file.
For your personal client key, use your own account as owner and restrict access to that account under workplace policy. Reading is enough for SSH to use it. Other ordinary users or shared groups should not read it. Do not copy Windows SSH server authorized_keys permission recipes onto this personal private key.
If the owner is another account, the file is centrally managed, or access is denied, stop and ask the Windows administrator to repair this exact file. Do not take ownership of a folder tree. If elevation is required, reopen PowerShell with Run as administrator under the intended identity and recheck whoami first.
Keep keys under %USERPROFILE%\.ssh, outside OneDrive and the repository. If this key is in a synced/shared folder, arrange a move to that local folder while preserving working access. After moving it, repeat the path-selection and inspection cards with its new path before continuing. Moving it does not erase older shared or cloud copies; replace an exposed key through your normal key-rotation process.
steps.command:
icacls "$SonicKey"
$SonicKeyFolder = [System.IO.Path]::GetDirectoryName($SonicKey)
icacls "$SonicKeyFolder"
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Owner
(Get-Acl -LiteralPath $SonicKey).Access | Select-Object IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited
steps.expected: You know the owner, your account SID and the exact unwanted entries before changing anything.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Save the current permissions before editing
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
This saves permission information, not the private-key contents. Keep the backup path in your local notes. /save saves the file’s access list; it is not a backup of the key and does not save its owner.
Push-Location temporarily opens the key’s parent folder so the saved filename can be restored to the same folder later. Pop-Location returns to your previous folder.
If saving fails, stop. Do not continue with an unknown recovery path.
steps.command:
$SonicAclFolder = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA "SONIC"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $SonicAclFolder -Force | Out-Null
$SonicAclBackup = Join-Path $SonicAclFolder ("key-acl-" + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString() + ".txt")
$SonicKeyName = [System.IO.Path]::GetFileName($SonicKey)
Push-Location -LiteralPath $SonicKeyFolder
icacls "$SonicKeyName" /save "$SonicAclBackup"
$SonicAclSaved = $LASTEXITCODE
Pop-Location
if ($SonicAclSaved -ne 0) { throw "ACL backup failed: stop" }
$SonicAclBackup
steps.expected: The permission backup was saved successfully and its path is recorded.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Give your own account read access, then remove inherited entries
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Use this only for the personally owned key checked above. Run one line at a time. /grant:r replaces the explicit Allow entry for this SID only. It does not remove other users, groups or Deny entries.
The * tells icacls that the value is a numeric SID. R gives read access. Adding your explicit entry first avoids removing your only inherited access.
/inheritance:r turns off inheritance and removes inherited entries from this file. It does not touch every file in the folder. Stop on any error.
steps.expected: Your explicit read entry exists. Review any remaining explicit entries in the next step.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Remove only a confirmed unwanted explicit entry
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
If the permission list still shows an unwanted account or group, copy its exact SID from the error or identify it with the Windows administrator. Do not enter your own SID. Do not remove entries from a whole folder tree.
S-1-5-32 identifies the Windows BUILTIN domain; it is not a universal name for every built-in group. Use the exact offending entry shown for your file. Do not copy another person’s account SID from a screenshot.
The command below removes entries for the chosen SID only. Run it once per reviewed unwanted entry, then inspect the list again. If the remaining entries are unclear or policy-managed, use the administrator rather than guessing.
GUI alternative: File Explorer → the exact key → right-click → Properties → Security → Advanced. Check Owner. Select only an unwanted permission entry → Remove. Keep your account’s Read entry → Apply → OK. Inspect again. Do not reset the whole folder.
Do not use /reset as the normal fix: it replaces the file’s permissions with inherited defaults and can make the key readable by others again.
steps.expected: Only the intended personal-key access remains. No shared group or unrelated user can read the key.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: Try SSH again with the recorded Linux username
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:
Enter the VM’s current public IP and the Linux username from its creation record. This course uses rexuser. If your own VM was created with a different name, use the verified name—not a guess based on the error.
Keep the path in quotes. -i selects this private key; IdentitiesOnly=yes prevents SSH from trying unrelated keys. Verify any host fingerprint against trusted notes. A passphrase prompt unlocks the local key; it is not an Azure password prompt.
If the too-open warning is gone but Permission denied remains, the local file fix worked and another check is needed. Verify the selected public key was installed for the recorded Linux account, then inspect that account’s server-side SSH settings through the approved recovery route. Do not disable host checking or switch usernames blindly.
steps.command:
$SonicVmAddress = Read-Host "VM public IP from Azure"
$SonicVmUser = Read-Host "Linux username from the VM build record"
ssh -i "$SonicKey" -o IdentitiesOnly=yes "$SonicVmUser@$SonicVmAddress"
steps.expected: The local key warning is gone. A successful Linux login is verified separately with whoami and hostname.

steps.lessonTitle: Make the first SSH connection as rexuser
steps.title: If a permission edit goes wrong, restore the saved access list
steps.where: Your own Windows computer · Windows Terminal → PowerShell · normal user
steps.action:

steps.expected: The saved access list is restored, or the exact restore error is recorded for the administrator.

steps.lessonTitle: Orient yourself in the home directory
steps.title: Command 3: read, type, then check
steps.where: Endpoint rhel9-lab-01 · connected SSH tab · RHEL Bash as rexuser
steps.action:
pwd prints the present working directory. A fresh rexuser login normally starts in /home/rexuser, but verify rather than assume.
ls lists directory entries; without a path it lists the current directory. -la combines -l (long details) and -a (all entries, including dotfiles).
Long output includes file type/permission bits, link count, owner, group, size, timestamp, and name. A leading d indicates a directory; . means this directory and .. means its parent.
A filename starting with . is hidden from ordinary ls. The .ssh directory is normally visible with -a. Hidden does not mean encrypted or inaccessible.
ssh-keygen -l displays public-key fingerprints; -f selects ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Bash expands ~ to rexuser’s home, normally /home/rexuser. This file is a list of authorized public keys, not the private file from Windows.
steps.expected: The current path, a long home-directory listing, and the fingerprint of the public key Azure authorized for rexuser. If multiple keys are intentionally authorized, multiple entries may appear.

steps.lessonTitle: Match the installation method to the artifact
steps.title: Command 1: read, type, then check
steps.where: Reference examples · commented, do not execute
steps.action:
# makes each example a shell comment. These placeholders demonstrate methods; they are not a request to install anything now.
chmod changes permission bits. u+x adds execute permission for the owner only. ./script.sh uses ./ to mean a file in the current directory, not one found through PATH. Review contents, source, integrity, and required interpreter before execution.
bash ./script.sh is an alternative that asks Bash to read the script; it normally needs read permission rather than an execute bit. It does not make a malicious script safe, and not every .sh file is meant for Bash.
sudo requests privileged execution. dnf install ./package.rpm installs a local RPM and resolves dependencies through configured repositories; ./ distinguishes the local file from a repository package name. Review package signature/source and the transaction before confirming.
tar handles archives. -t lists members, -x extracts, -z processes gzip compression, and -f says the next argument is the archive filename. Use listing before extraction and an empty staging directory; untrusted paths, links, or overwrite targets need review. Extraction alone does not install software.
Repository-based dnf install package-name selects a named package from enabled repositories. Trust the repository and package signatures, inspect the proposed transaction, and record the exact installed version.
steps.command:
# Reviewed shell script, two alternative invocation methods:
# chmod u+x ./script.sh
# ./script.sh
# OR: bash ./script.sh
# Reviewed local RPM:
# sudo dnf install ./package.rpm
# Inspect archive before extraction:
# tar -tzf archive.tar.gz
# tar -xzf archive.tar.gz
# Approved repository package:
# sudo dnf install package-name
steps.expected: You can explain the correct method and inspection requirements for each artifact type without changing system state.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: Before anything changes: decide exactly what to back up
steps.where: Work administration workstation · change record and Veeam console (12 or 13)
steps.action:
Start with the VM you will change: select its whole-VM backup, including the OS disk and every data disk used by the application. For a new RHEL installation, back up the clean, working VM before installing Wazuh. After successful installation and verification, create a new accepted baseline; retain the pre-change recovery point according to policy.
If the change affects AD, DNS, domain membership or Group Policy, verify a recent application-aware backup of the domain controller first, including the volumes containing AD DS, SYSVOL and DNS-related state. Record domain-recovery access and the approved AD recovery procedure. A DNS export or GPO export alone cannot recover a domain controller. Do not casually revert a production domain controller snapshot.
For the Wazuh central host, include its OS, configuration, certificates, enrollment material and all disks containing indexer/event data. If manager, indexer and dashboard are separate VMs, identify all of them. A live disk copy is not automatically a consistent Wazuh/indexer backup: use the application recovery procedure or a coordinated clean shutdown in an approved outage. Do not independently restore mismatched cluster members.
For the RHEL endpoint or Windows client, include the OS, application data and agent configuration before agent installation, realm changes or hardening. Record its current manager association so recovery does not leave duplicate or stale enrollment. Back up only the affected systems and dependencies; an endpoint-only change does not require backing up every enterprise VM.
Save a protected change record outside the changed VM: hostnames, IP/DNS settings, disk inventory, package/kernel versions, service status, relevant configuration and rollback triggers. Keep credentials, private keys and recovery passwords in approved secret storage, never in the course GitHub repository. File hashes and screenshots are evidence, not backups.
steps.expected: A named list of affected VMs, all required disks, dependencies and application-consistency requirements exists before a backup job is selected.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: Verify the backup scope and recovery access before taking a snapshot
steps.where: Veeam Backup & Replication 12/13 · console
steps.action:
Open Home → Jobs → Backup. Select the existing job → Edit. On Virtual Machines, confirm the exact VM is included; inspect exclusions and disk selection so required data disks are not omitted. Inspect Storage for the intended repository and retention. Use Cancel after read-only inspection; have the backup owner apply any required job changes.
For a Windows domain controller, inspect Guest Processing → application-aware processing and the per-VM application settings. Confirm guest credentials and processing success in the completed session, rather than merely seeing a checked option. Windows AD processing does not make an arbitrary Linux application consistent.
Check that the backup repository is outside the VM being changed, has capacity and remains reachable during recovery. Confirm the restore operator can access the backup and its encryption password independently of the affected machine/domain. Follow the workplace policy for an independent protected or immutable copy.
Ask the backup owner to verify the Veeam server configuration backup too. In the main menu select Configuration Backup and inspect its latest success, repository and encryption setting. This protects backup configuration; it does not replace VM backups. Store its encryption password separately in approved storage. Do not change enterprise backup settings as part of an endpoint lesson.
Run the approved VM backup using the later cards, verify the new per-VM restore point, and record a tested restore route. Only then take a short-lived vSphere snapshot immediately before the change if required. Backup first, temporary snapshot second, change third. This is a pre-change protection order, not a universal disaster-recovery restore order.
steps.expected: The current restore point covers the intended data, recovery access works, and application-specific restore limitations are recorded. Unknown coverage is a no-go.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: At work: select the exact vSphere VM and recovery scope
steps.where: Work administration workstation · vSphere Client
steps.action:
Sign in to the approved vCenter URL. Open Menu → VMs and Templates. Select the intended RHEL VM and compare its name, folder, host and disks with the change record. Do not act on a similarly named production VM.
Open Snapshots → Manage Snapshots and inspect existing checkpoints. Check datastore free space and whether a backup job is running. Coordinate the maintenance window with the backup owner; do not take or remove a checkpoint during an active backup.
Record change scope, rollback trigger, maximum diagnosis time, snapshot expiry, backup restore point and validation steps. This RHEL procedure is not a domain-controller recovery procedure: AD needs application-aware/system-state recovery planning and identity consistency.
steps.expected: The change targets one identified RHEL VM and has an independent backup/recovery plan.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: At work: create a short-lived vSphere snapshot
steps.where: Work administration workstation · vSphere Client
steps.action:
Right-click the selected VM → Snapshots → Take Snapshot. Enter a unique name containing the change ID and time, and a description of the pre-change state.
For a planned cold checkpoint, shut down the guest cleanly first and confirm Powered off. Memory capture does not apply while powered off. For an approved powered-on checkpoint, decide whether memory capture is needed; it increases size/time. Filesystem quiescing requires working VMware Tools and is not automatically application-consistent backup.
Select Create/OK. Watch Recent Tasks until the snapshot task succeeds, then reopen Manage Snapshots to confirm its name/time. Record the evidence before starting the change.
Keep snapshots brief and remove them after validation and approval. Broadcom advises not retaining a single snapshot beyond 72 hours; workplace policy can require a shorter period. Snapshot deltas depend on base disks, so they are not standalone backups.
steps.expected: The intended checkpoint exists and its owner, expiry and consistency limitations are recorded.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: At work: choose fix, revert or restore from backup
steps.where: Work administration workstation · change record and vSphere Client
steps.action:
If the change works, validate the application and document the result. If it fails, preserve logs and make one evidence-based correction within the agreed time. If risk grows or the time expires, stop and execute the recorded recovery branch.
For an approved snapshot revert: right-click the exact VM → Snapshots → Manage Snapshots. Select the recorded pre-change checkpoint → Revert. Read the warning about losing later changes and confirm only within the approved outage/data-loss scope. Verify power state, guest access, storage and application behavior afterward.
For cleanup after a successful change: select the checkpoint → Delete. Deleting merges snapshot changes; it does not restore the earlier state. Monitor the task and datastore capacity. Do not select Delete All merely to remove one checkpoint.
If snapshots cannot meet the recovery requirement, use the enterprise backup restore plan. Test a recovery to an isolated destination when possible; never connect a duplicate restored identity to production by accident.
steps.expected: Recovery is judged by validated guest/application state, not just a completed hypervisor task.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: At work: identify the Veeam product and supported commands
steps.where: Approved Veeam administration machine · Veeam PowerShell session
steps.action:
Open the Veeam console → Help → About and record the product, version and build. These command names refer to Veeam Backup & Replication VMware VM jobs; Veeam Agent jobs and other Veeam products use different cmdlets.
Open the PowerShell session supplied with the installed Veeam console. Run Get-Command to discover what is available, then Get-Help for the local syntax. Do not run these in the RHEL terminal or assume ordinary Windows PowerShell already has the Veeam module.
Get-VBRJob inspects VM jobs; Get-VBRBackupSession inspects execution history; Get-VBRRestorePoint inspects recovery points. Starting a job is a separate authorized operation, not proof of recovery. The exact start/restore walkthrough must match your workplace version and job type.
steps.command:
Get-Command Get-VBRJob, Get-VBRBackupSession, Get-VBRRestorePoint, Start-VBRJob
Get-Help Get-VBRJob -Full
Get-Help Start-VBRJob -Full
steps.expected: The product/build and supported local command syntax are identified before any backup job is changed or started.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: At work: inspect one existing VMware backup job
steps.where: Veeam Backup & Replication · Veeam PowerShell session
steps.action:
This example targets an existing VMware VM backup job, not a Veeam Agent policy. Verify these cmdlets in your installed version first. In the console select Home → Jobs → Backup and copy the exact approved job name.
Enter that name at the prompt. Get-VBRJob retrieves jobs; Where-Object keeps only an exact name match. The count check stops an ambiguous selection. Review the returned job in the console and confirm it includes the intended VM, the correct repository, retention and application-processing settings.
Get-VBRBackupSession lists history. It does not create a backup. Inspect the job session and per-VM task results in History; an old successful run is not proof of a current restore point.
steps.command:
$SonicJobName = Read-Host "Exact approved VMware backup job name"
$SonicJobs = @(Get-VBRJob | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq $SonicJobName })
if ($SonicJobs.Count -ne 1) { throw "Expected exactly one job: stop" }
$SonicJob = $SonicJobs[0]
$SonicJob | Format-List Name, JobType
Get-VBRBackupSession | Sort-Object CreationTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 JobName, CreationTime, EndTime, State, Result
steps.expected: One reviewed job is selected and its VM membership and recent task results are understood.

steps.lessonTitle: Checkpoint: what is your rollback plan?
steps.title: At work: run the approved backup and verify recovery evidence

steps.action:

Open Home → Backups → Disk, expand the backup and locate the intended VM. Inspect its restore points and record the new timestamp, repository and retention. Arrange an isolated restore rehearsal under the workplace restore procedure; a successful backup job alone does not prove bootability or application recovery.
Exact restore wizard choices depend on your Veeam version, destination and workload. Record these with the backup owner before the change; do not improvise an in-place production restore. Return to the rollback gate only when the documented recovery objective is achievable.
steps.expected: The intended VM has a verified new restore point and a documented, tested recovery path. No infrastructure command is executed by the course itself.

steps.title: Prevent an accidental Wazuh upgrade
steps.where: RHEL manager · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
First inspect the repository file. If it does not exist at this path, stop and identify the actual repo file; do not create an unrelated one.
Copy a metadata-preserving checkpoint using cp -a -n; -n avoids replacing an earlier backup. sed -i edits the file in place and changes an exact enabled=1 line to enabled=0. The final grep shows the enabled settings. This affects only the Wazuh repo, not RHEL repositories.
steps.command:
sudo cat /etc/yum.repos.d/wazuh.repo
sudo cp -an /etc/yum.repos.d/wazuh.repo /etc/yum.repos.d/wazuh.repo.sonic-before-disable
sudo sed -i "s/^enabled=1/enabled=0/" /etc/yum.repos.d/wazuh.repo
sudo grep -n "enabled=" /etc/yum.repos.d/wazuh.repo
steps.expected: The Wazuh repository section shows enabled=0; the backup remains available for a deliberately approved upgrade.

steps.action:
status reports runtime state; --no-pager avoids interactive scrolling. ss -lntp lists listening TCP sockets with numeric addresses and owning processes.
If a unit fails, run sudo journalctl -u followed by that exact unit name and --since "10 minutes ago" --no-pager. Read the earliest relevant error before changing network rules.

steps.title: Add narrowly scoped Azure HTTPS access
steps.where: Windows workstation · Azure Portal
steps.action:
Use the workstation’s current public IPv4 used for outbound connections from your restricted-SSH record; verify it is still current. Write it with /32. This is not the workstation’s private LAN address.
Open manager VM → Networking → Network settings → its NSG → Inbound security rules → Add. Set Source to IP Addresses, Source IP to that workstation /32, Source port ranges to *, Destination to the manager private IP, Service to Custom, Destination port to 443, Protocol TCP, Action Allow.
Choose an unused priority that precedes a blocking rule; lower numbers take precedence. Name the rule sonic-dashboard-workstation and select Add. Record the priority. Check NIC and subnet effective rules; preserve SSH and investigate any existing broad allow rather than assuming this rule removes it.
steps.expected: Effective rules permit the workstation’s HTTPS traffic without adding Internet-wide application access.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Inspect the guest firewall before testing
steps.where: RHEL manager · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
is-active checks whether firewalld runs. If inactive, record that state; do not enable it blindly during installation. If active, the next command identifies the zone attached to the manager NIC.
Run sudo firewall-cmd --zone= followed by the actual zone and --list-all. Compare existing services, ports and rich rules. If HTTPS is blocked, use the source-restricted rule procedure in the next card; otherwise skip that change.
steps.expected: The active zone and relevant allow rules are known.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: If required, allow the workstation in the active zone
steps.where: RHEL manager · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Only use this card when firewalld is active and the earlier check showed the rule missing. Enter the exact zone and workstation /32 at the prompts.
The rich rule accepts IPv4 TCP 443 from that source. Apply it at runtime first, test HTTPS in the browser, then run the permanent line only after the test succeeds. --permanent stores the same rule for future starts; do not reload unrelated rules.
To undo this specific addition, rerun the two add-rich-rule commands with remove-rich-rule in place of add-rich-rule, using the same variables.
steps.command:
read -r -p "Active zone: " SONIC_ZONE
read -r -p "Workstation public IPv4/32: " SONIC_SOURCE
SONIC_RULE="rule family=ipv4 source address=$SONIC_SOURCE port port=443 protocol=tcp accept"
sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$SONIC_RULE"
steps.expected: The runtime rule is added. Test the browser and save it only at the later persistence checkpoint.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Compare the dashboard certificate
steps.where: RHEL manager · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Read the configured server.ssl.certificate path. At the prompt paste that path without its YAML quote characters. openssl x509 reads that certificate; -noout omits certificate content and -fingerprint -sha256 prints its SHA-256 identity.
In Windows, open https:// plus the manager public IP. On a certificate warning, inspect the certificate details and SHA-256 fingerprint. Compare with the trusted SSH result. Approve a lab exception only when it is the intended certificate; a mismatch is a stop condition.
steps.command:
sudo grep -n "server.ssl.certificate" /etc/wazuh-dashboard/opensearch_dashboards.yml
read -r -p "Configured certificate path: " SONIC_CERT
sudo openssl x509 -in "$SONIC_CERT" -noout -fingerprint -sha256
steps.expected: The browser certificate matches the certificate configured on this manager.

Wait for the application to load. Open the navigation menu and agent/endpoint inventory. Check for API/indexer errors. A new manager can have no remote agents yet; that is expected at this stage.
steps.expected: An authenticated dashboard loads without central-connection errors. No endpoint check-in is claimed yet.

steps.where: RHEL manager · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Skip this card if you did not add a runtime rule. Return to the same manager Bash tab, where SONIC_ZONE and SONIC_RULE still hold the reviewed values. After browser authentication succeeds, save that exact rule permanently. If the tab was closed, re-enter and inspect the original values before running this command.
--permanent saves the rule for future firewalld starts. --list-rich-rules shows the saved rules; compare with the runtime rule and source restriction.
steps.expected: The tested source-restricted rule is saved without reloading unrelated firewall settings.
