steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Choose one device or an approved subnet
steps.where: Work Windows computer · network plan
steps.action:
One IPv4 address uses /32, such as 192.0.2.50/32. A subnet is a range, such as 10.20.30.0/24. These are examples only. Get the real source range and approval from the network owner.
A vSphere port group is not itself an IP subnet. Confirm the VLAN, subnet and routing used by the VMs attached to it. Allowing a subnet allows any device with a matching source address, not just VMs with a particular port-group name.
If the manager also runs in vSphere, there is no Azure NSG on that VM. Review RHEL firewalld and the actual network/NSX firewalls. If the manager is in Azure, also review its NSGs.
With private routed connectivity to Azure, use the private source range only if that range is actually preserved. With a public internet connection, Azure normally sees the company firewall’s translated public address. Use the confirmed public address or addresses, not an unreachable private range. One shared public address can represent devices outside the intended port group too.
steps.expected: You know the source address the manager really sees. You are changing dashboard HTTPS access only, not SSH access.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Inspect the RHEL firewall before adding a rule
steps.where: Wazuh manager · connected RHEL Bash session · rexuser
steps.action:
Keep your working administration connection open. Run the checks below. Confirm firewalld is running and identify the active zone for dashboard traffic. A source-based zone can take precedence over an interface zone, so review both. Do not assume the zone is public.
Write down existing runtime and permanent settings. Look for broad HTTPS service entries, port 443 openings, rich rules, policies, or trusted zones. Adding a narrow Allow rule does not cancel a broader Allow rule.
steps.command:
hostname
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --list-all-zones
steps.expected: You know the correct zone and existing rules. If the firewall is not running, review the actual firewall system before proceeding.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Add one temporary HTTPS rule
steps.where: Wazuh manager · connected RHEL Bash session · rexuser
steps.action:
At the first prompt, enter the verified zone name. At the second, choose either one actual address ending in /32 or the approved actual subnet range. Use only one choice for this change.
The same command handles both choices. For example, source address="192.0.2.50/32" selects one address, while source address="10.20.30.0/24" selects that subnet. The port remains 443 and the protocol remains TCP.
This first rule is runtime-only and expires after ten minutes. Do not add a public-wide source. The checks below only confirm the rule was added; they do not prove other sources are blocked.
steps.command:
read -r -p "Verified firewalld zone: " SONIC_ZONE
read -r -p "Approved source IPv4/32 OR subnet/CIDR: " SONIC_SOURCE
printf -v SONIC_HTTPS_RULE 'rule family="ipv4" source address="%s" port port="443" protocol="tcp" accept' "$SONIC_SOURCE"
sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE" --timeout=10m
sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --query-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE"
steps.expected: The rule is accepted and query returns yes. Do not continue if a command reports an error.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Match the network rule and test from real clients
steps.where: Work Windows computer · browser and approved network console
steps.action:
For an Azure manager: open Azure → the manager VM → Networking → its actual network security group → Inbound security rules. Open the existing dashboard TCP 443 rule. Save its old source in your notes. Set Source to IP Addresses and enter the actual source address/range selected above. Keep TCP 443 and Allow. Save. Do not edit the SSH rule or reuse an occupied priority for a second rule.
For a vSphere manager: ask the network owner to allow the same source-to-manager TCP 443 path in the firewall or NSX policy that actually applies. A port-group setting alone is not a dashboard firewall rule.
From an allowed client, open the dashboard URL and verify its certificate before sign-in. For a subnet, test more than one intended client. Also test an approved client outside the allowed range. If it can still connect, inspect the broader existing rules; the new narrow rule is not an exclusive restriction.
Do not save the temporary RHEL change permanently until allowed clients work and the intended restrictions are confirmed. If it expires while you investigate, that is expected; review the result before re-adding it.
steps.expected: Allowed clients can reach HTTPS. An approved outside-range test confirms the intended restriction. SSH remains available.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Save the tested rule, or undo this change
steps.where: Wazuh manager · connected RHEL Bash session · rexuser
steps.action:
Success branch: run the permanent add below only after the client tests pass. It saves this rule for future reloads/restarts. The temporary runtime rule still expires, so schedule a controlled reload from the reviewed permanent configuration and retest. Keep recovery access; a reload also discards other runtime-only changes.
Failure branch: do not run the save command. Let the temporary rule expire, or remove this exact runtime rule using --remove-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE" with the same zone. Restore the old source in the network/NSG rule if that was changed.
To remove this saved rule later, use sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$SONIC_ZONE" --remove-rich-rule="$SONIC_HTTPS_RULE", then follow the controlled reload and test procedure. Remove only a rule added by this change. Do not remove an old working single-IP rule until the new approved access is verified.
steps.expected: The exact approved rule is saved. The next card applies and checks the permanent configuration.

steps.lessonTitle: Discover services and validate dashboard access
steps.title: Apply the reviewed permanent rules and check again
steps.where: Wazuh manager · connected RHEL Bash session · rexuser
steps.action:
Proceed only on the successful save branch and in the approved change window. Check the permanent configuration, then reload. Keep the console/recovery path ready.
Confirm the rich rule is present again and repeat the allowed and outside-range browser tests. Record the final source range, zone and network rule. A firewall rule permits a connection; dashboard users still need their own approved sign-in access.
steps.command:
sudo firewall-cmd --check-config

steps.lessonTitle: Verify the endpoint RPM before installation
steps.title: Download and validate on Windows before transfer
steps.where: Windows workstation · PowerShell
steps.action:
Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell. Create a staging folder under your local profile. Paste the exact official RPM URL and the separate vendor SHA-512 value at the prompts. The digest must contain 128 hexadecimal characters; paste only the digest, not the filename.
Invoke-WebRequest downloads without executing the RPM. Get-FileHash calculates SHA-512 over the downloaded bytes. The comparison ignores hexadecimal letter case. Stop on an exception: check filename, release, architecture and algorithm, then download again from the official source. Never change the expected digest to make a failed check pass.
A vendor checksum checks against published bytes; it does not replace the signing-key and RPM signature checks below. Keep the digest in your change record.
steps.command:
$SonicStage = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE "sonic-artifacts"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $SonicStage | Out-Null
$SonicRpm = Join-Path $SonicStage "wazuh-agent.rpm"
$SonicUrl = Read-Host "Exact official HTTPS RPM URL"
$SonicExpected = (Read-Host "Vendor SHA-512 digest only").Trim()
if ($SonicUrl -notmatch "^https://packages\.wazuh\.com/") { throw "Use the official package URL" }
if ($SonicExpected -notmatch "^[0-9a-fA-F]{128}$") { throw "Invalid SHA-512 value" }
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $SonicUrl -OutFile $SonicRpm
$SonicActual = (Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $SonicRpm -Algorithm SHA512).Hash
if ($SonicActual -ine $SonicExpected) { throw "CHECKSUM MISMATCH: do not transfer or install" }
Write-Output "VENDOR SHA-512 MATCH"
$SonicActual
steps.expected: VENDOR SHA-512 MATCH appears before you transfer anything.

steps.expected: Exactly one recovery branch is selected and its evidence/retention requirements are understood.

steps.lessonTitle: Restore and validate the approved endpoint baseline
steps.title: Branch A only: remove the reviewed agent package
steps.where: RHEL endpoint · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Skip this card for disk restore. Stop the agent, then inspect DNF’s removal list. Enter y only if the proposed removal matches the approved endpoint-agent scope; otherwise enter n.
After removal, rpm should report not installed. list-unit-files shows any remaining definitions. ls reports residual directories or “No such file or directory”; either outcome must be recorded.
Do not delete /var/ossec recursively. Retain remaining keys/configuration under restricted permissions until the owner approves exact cleanup; never use this endpoint procedure on the manager.
steps.command:
sudo systemctl stop wazuh-agent
sudo dnf remove wazuh-agent
rpm -q wazuh-agent
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --no-pager
sudo ls -ld /var/ossec /var/ossec/etc
steps.expected: The package is absent; residual files and units are recorded rather than silently discarded.

steps.lessonTitle: Restore and validate the approved endpoint baseline
steps.title: Branch B only: create the recovery disk
steps.where: Windows workstation · Azure Portal
steps.action:
Skip this card for package removal. Search Virtual machines → rhel9-lab-01 → Stop. Wait for Stopped (deallocated). Record the current OS disk resource ID from Disks.
Search Snapshots → select the exact approved endpoint pre-install snapshot → Create disk. Enter a distinct recovery disk name and the recorded subscription/resource group/region. Match the original VM’s disk compatibility, zone and encryption requirements; review cost and Create.
Wait for deployment success. Open the new disk and record its resource ID. If the source snapshot, OS type, generation or encryption is wrong, stop before swapping. Do not delete the old OS disk.
steps.expected: A compatible managed recovery disk exists from the intended endpoint snapshot.

steps.lessonTitle: Restore and validate the approved endpoint baseline
steps.title: Branch B only: swap and start the endpoint
steps.where: Windows workstation · Azure Portal
steps.action:
Open the deallocated endpoint VM → Disks → Swap OS disk. Choose the newly created recovery disk. Type the VM name when asked to confirm, then select OK.
If the intended disk is absent from the list, stop and check region/compatibility rather than choosing another disk. After success, return to Overview → Start and wait for Running.
Record the current public IP and reconnect from PowerShell with the retained SSH key. Verify the fingerprint against trusted-console evidence if it changed. Keep the displaced disk until recovery validation passes.
steps.expected: The endpoint boots from the recovery disk and rexuser access is verified.

steps.lessonTitle: Restore and validate the approved endpoint baseline
steps.title: Remove only the retired endpoint registration
steps.where: RHEL manager · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Confirm the manager hostname. manage_agents -l lists agent identities. Match the exact ID with the endpoint evidence; never remove ID 000.
Start the interactive manager tool. At its menu choose R to remove an agent; enter the exact endpoint ID; read the displayed name/address and confirm only if they match the intentionally retired endpoint. Choose Q to quit. Menu wording can vary; use the displayed remove/quit options.
This branch expects a pre-agent snapshot or removed agent. If a restored disk is already enrolled and monitoring is meant to continue, do not remove that record; reconcile the restored identity with the owner instead.
steps.expected: The manager registration state matches the chosen rollback outcome; unrelated agents remain.

steps.lessonTitle: Restore and validate the approved endpoint baseline
steps.title: Validate the restored guest against its baseline
steps.where: RHEL endpoint · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Check account/host first. Compare failed units, mounts, capacity, routes and SELinux with the saved pre-change values. Missing Wazuh is expected for this pre-agent rollback, not a new fault.
Compare Azure NIC/NSG rules with the saved record. Remove only lab-created agent-specific rules if they are no longer needed; select the exact named rule → Delete → confirm its scope. Keep restricted SSH access.
Record residual differences explicitly. A successful boot or package removal alone does not finish this check.
steps.command:
whoami
hostname
cat /etc/redhat-release
rpm -q wazuh-agent
systemctl --failed --no-pager
findmnt
df -h
ip route
getenforce
steps.expected: The baseline comparisons and central registration disposition are documented.

steps.lessonTitle: Restore and validate the approved endpoint baseline
steps.title: Save evidence before marking this lesson verified
steps.where: Windows workstation · your lab notes
steps.action:
Record chosen recovery branch, baseline comparisons, endpoint enrollment disposition, retained disk/snapshot IDs and residual exceptions. Include the host and date/time.
Capture only the relevant result area. Exclude credentials, private keys, enrollment keys and secret-bearing logs. Compare your result with the expected result; if it differs, use the troubleshooting section below and leave the lesson unverified.
steps.expected: Your notes contain the actual observation and enough context to distinguish it from example output.

steps.lessonTitle: Close the change with evidence and cost control
steps.title: Complete the change record
steps.where: Windows workstation · lab notes
steps.action:
Create these headings: Scope; Hosts; Versions and artifact trust; Configuration changes; Successful event evidence; Fault and root cause; Recovery branch; Final state; Exceptions; Retention and costs.
Under each heading paste your redacted observations from the earlier lessons. Include actual timestamps and resource/agent IDs. State whether the endpoint agent is removed, restored pre-install, or subsequently re-enrolled; do not simply write “healthy.”
steps.expected: Each acceptance result has evidence and the final monitoring state is explicit.

steps.lessonTitle: Close the change with evidence and cost control
steps.title: Check both hosts before shutdown
steps.where: Both RHEL SSH tabs · Bash · rexuser
steps.action:
Run this block separately in each host tab. Label each result with hostname/date. Compare failed units, mounts and capacity with the recorded baseline.
If an unexplained failure remains, record it as an open exception and keep the change open. Do not conceal it by marking every lesson complete.
steps.expected: Both hosts have a documented final observation.

steps.lessonTitle: Close the change with evidence and cost control
steps.title: Deallocate the endpoint and manager
steps.where: Windows workstation · Azure Portal
steps.action:
Save your work and type exit in each SSH tab to close its remote session.
Search Virtual machines → select rhel9-lab-01 → Stop → confirm. Wait for Stopped (deallocated). Repeat for rhel9-manager-01 and confirm its state independently.
Capture the VM list showing both states, without credentials or unnecessary account details. A guest shutdown alone may leave allocated resources.
steps.expected: Both VMs show Stopped (deallocated).

steps.lessonTitle: Close the change with evidence and cost control
steps.title: Review retained resources and hand off
steps.where: Windows workstation · Azure Portal
steps.action:
Open the lab resource group → Resources. List retained OS/data disks, snapshots, public IPs and other billable resources in your notes. Deallocation does not delete them or eliminate all charges.
For each recovery artifact record its resource ID, retention end date and owner decision. Keep it while any rollback issue is unresolved. Do not delete resources merely to make the list empty.
Review your notes for passwords, private keys and secret-bearing logs; remove those from the shared copy. Mark the lesson verified only after the final state and open exceptions are accurately recorded.
steps.expected: The handoff explains the lab outcome, retained costs and recovery responsibilities.

steps.lessonTitle: Close the change with evidence and cost control
steps.title: Save evidence before marking this lesson verified
steps.where: Windows workstation · your lab notes
steps.action:
Record final state of each host, both deallocated statuses, resource-retention decisions and redacted change record. Include the host and date/time.
Capture only the relevant result area. Exclude credentials, private keys, enrollment keys and secret-bearing logs. Compare your result with the expected result; if it differs, use the troubleshooting section below and leave the lesson unverified.
steps.expected: Your notes contain the actual observation and enough context to distinguish it from example output.

steps.lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
steps.title: List what you need every day
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Write down browser, email, office documents, meetings, printers, games, VPN, and any Windows-only programs. Mark each as native Linux, web, or requires Windows.
steps.expected: You have a short compatibility checklist before installation.

steps.lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
steps.title: Choose the baseline
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Use the current supported AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 DVD ISO for this course and select Server with GUI during installation. The title says Server, but this profile supplies GNOME. AlmaLinux 10 may have different hardware and package support.
steps.expected: Your notes identify major version 9 and GNOME.

steps.lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
steps.title: Protect your current machine
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Back up important files to a separate device or service and restore one sample. Save recovery keys for existing encrypted disks privately. Start with a new VM; do not repartition your Windows system.
steps.expected: The restored sample opens and the existing OS remains untouched.

steps.lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
steps.title: Size the practice VM
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Plan 2 virtual CPU cores, 4 GB RAM minimum for this exercise (8 GB if your host can spare it), a new 50 GB virtual disk, and NAT networking. Leave resources for Windows.
steps.expected: The host can run one GNOME VM without exhausting RAM or storage.

steps.lessonTitle: Plan Your Everyday Linux Desktop
steps.title: Plan a later physical installation
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Only after validating the VM, test a live environment if available and consult the current installation guide for Wi-Fi, audio, GPU, printers, encryption and disk layout. Keep backups and Windows recovery media.
steps.expected: You have a hardware test list and a recovery route.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Verify the downloaded ISO
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Download the DVD ISO and CHECKSUM from almalinux.org using official mirror links. In Windows PowerShell compute its SHA-256 and compare with the exact filename in CHECKSUM; check official signature guidance when available. Replace the example ISO path in the command with the exact file you downloaded.
steps.expected: The complete SHA-256 matches the official checksum for your downloaded ISO.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Create a fresh VM
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In VMware Workstation Pro choose File → New Virtual Machine → Typical → I will install the operating system later. Choose a compatible RHEL 9 64-bit guest profile (or AlmaLinux 9 if offered), name ALMA-DESKTOP, and create a NEW 50 GB virtual disk.
steps.expected: A new VM appears in the library with a blank disk.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Attach media and networking
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Before power-on open VM Settings. Set 2 cores and your planned RAM. On CD/DVD attach the verified AlmaLinux 9 DVD ISO and enable Connect at power on. On Network Adapter select NAT.
steps.expected: The VM summary shows the correct ISO, memory, and NAT.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Start the installer
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Power on and select Test this media & install AlmaLinux 9 if available. Choose your language, keyboard and time zone on Installation Summary.
steps.expected: You reach the installer summary without a media-check error.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Select GNOME and the correct disk
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open Software Selection and choose Server with GUI. Open Installation Destination, select ONLY the new 50 GB virtual disk, and use automatic partitioning for this disposable VM. Review any pending deletion list before accepting.
steps.expected: Only the new VM disk is selected and Server with GUI is the software profile.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Create your daily user
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open User Creation, choose your own username and strong password, and enable Make this user administrator (wheel privileges). Keep root credentials private if you set them. Enable the NAT interface in Network & Host Name, then begin installation.
steps.expected: The installer accepts a normal administrative user and completes.

steps.lessonTitle: Install AlmaLinux with GNOME
steps.title: Boot the installed system
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Reboot when prompted, detach the ISO if it starts setup again, and sign in to GNOME as your normal user. Open Activities, search Terminal, and inspect the release.
steps.expected: The guest reports AlmaLinux 9 and opens a GNOME desktop.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
steps.title: Set the basics
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open Settings from the system menu. In Displays choose a readable resolution; in Keyboard/Region & Language verify layout; in Sound select output and test it. In Power choose sensible screen blanking.
steps.expected: Typing, display scaling and sound suit your setup.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
steps.title: Confirm networking
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Settings → Network inspect the wired connection. NAT normally supplies DHCP and DNS. Inspect addresses and routes without changing them.
steps.command:
ip -br address
ip route
nmcli device status
steps.expected: You have an address and default route for the VM NAT connection.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
steps.title: Update the guest
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Terminal refresh package metadata and review the proposed update transaction before accepting. Save work, then reboot when the update finishes.
steps.expected: The transaction completes without unresolved errors and GNOME returns after reboot.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
steps.title: Install VMware desktop integration
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Inspect/install the distribution guest tools. Review the transaction, then log out and back in or reboot. Keep shared folders and host clipboard sharing off unless you intentionally need them.
steps.expected: GNOME can resize appropriately when supported by your Workstation settings.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
steps.title: Set lock and privacy
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Settings → Privacy configure Screen Lock. Review Location and file-history options. Press Super+L and confirm the lock screen, then unlock with your own password.
steps.expected: The desktop locks and unlocks as expected.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Your Desktop
steps.title: Record a clean baseline
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open About and note release, memory and disk. Shut down the VM, then take a named Workstation snapshot if your edition supports it; separately keep backups of important files.
steps.expected: You have a baseline note and a VM recovery checkpoint.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Know where you are
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open Terminal and inspect your identity and location. Read each command and output before moving on. ~ means your home directory, not the whole filesystem.
steps.expected: You recognize your own username, host and home path.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Make a practice folder
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Create a practice folder under your home and move into it. mkdir -p creates missing parent directories. Use Tab to complete names and the Up arrow to recall a command.
steps.expected: pwd ends with DesktopPractice and the folder is inside your home.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Create, copy and rename
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Write two lines to a practice text file. > replaces that named file; do not aim it at valuable files. Copy first, then rename the copy.
steps.command:
cd ~/DesktopPractice
printf "first line\nsecond line\n" > notes.txt
cp -i notes.txt copy.txt
mv -i copy.txt renamed.txt
cat renamed.txt
steps.expected: You have notes.txt and renamed.txt with the same two lines.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Search and inspect
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Find files and filter text. A pipe sends one command’s output into the next. Use less to page through longer output and press q to leave.
steps.command:
cd ~/DesktopPractice
grep -n "second" notes.txt
wc -l notes.txt
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f
ls -lah | less
steps.expected: grep returns the matching line and wc counts two lines.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Learn help and interruption
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Use --help or man for syntax; q exits man. Ctrl+C interrupts a foreground task; Ctrl+Shift+C copies selected text in GNOME Terminal. Never paste a command you cannot explain.
steps.expected: You can find an option’s meaning and exit a pager.

steps.lessonTitle: Learn the Commands You Use Every Day
steps.title: Clean only your practice copy
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Use interactive removal for the renamed practice copy. Confirm only after checking its full path, then verify the original remains. Avoid rm -rf as a routine cleanup habit.
steps.expected: notes.txt remains and the chosen practice copy is gone.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Navigate with Files
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open Files from Activities. Open Home, Documents and Downloads. Ctrl+L enters a path; type ~/DesktopPractice and Enter. Ctrl+H toggles hidden files.
steps.expected: You can locate the same practice file from GUI and Terminal.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Create and organize
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Files create an Everyday folder in Documents. Copy notes.txt into it, rename the copy, and open it with the text editor. Use Trash for unwanted practice copies.
steps.expected: Your copied document opens and the original is still present.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Understand permissions
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Inspect a file you own. Apply mode 600 to the practice notes only: owner read/write, no access for group/others. This is not full-disk encryption.
steps.expected: ls shows owner-only read/write on that practice file.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Create an archive
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Use Files → right-click the Everyday folder → Compress (menu labels can vary). Choose a ZIP filename. Extract it into a temporary folder and open the copied note.
steps.expected: The extracted note matches your original.

steps.lessonTitle: Manage Files and Permissions
steps.title: Use removable storage
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Connect a USB data drive and open its entry in Files. Copy a harmless sample, wait for transfer completion, then use Eject/Unmount before disconnecting.
steps.expected: The sample reopens and the drive disconnects without a busy warning.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Inspect your existing software sources
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: DNF manages system RPMs and dependencies. GNOME Software may show RPM and Flatpak sources. List enabled DNF repositories and inspect package details before installing.
steps.command:
dnf repolist
dnf info firefox
dnf search libreoffice
steps.expected: You know which repositories are currently enabled.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Install a native everyday app
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: For an office suite use the AlmaLinux repository package libreoffice if available. Read the package source, dependencies and download size, then approve the install. Start it from Activities.
steps.expected: A document opens in the installed app.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Install Flatpak support
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Install the Flatpak client from your configured AlmaLinux repositories. Then inspect existing user remotes. System and user remotes are different scopes.
steps.command:
sudo dnf install flatpak
flatpak --version
flatpak remotes --user
steps.expected: flatpak is available and your user remote list is visible.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Add Flathub only after reviewing the source
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open the official Flathub AlmaLinux setup page linked below. If you accept this third-party source, add it to your user only. Inspect its URL afterward.
steps.expected: The user-scoped flathub remote points to the official source.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Install an app and review permissions
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Search for VLC, inspect the exact Flathub app ID and source, then install the user-scoped example only if you accept its publisher and permissions. Launch from Activities or Terminal.
steps.command:
flatpak search VLC
flatpak remote-info --user flathub org.videolan.VLC
flatpak install --user flathub org.videolan.VLC
flatpak info --user --show-permissions org.videolan.VLC
flatpak run org.videolan.VLC
steps.expected: VLC starts and opens a non-sensitive local media sample.

steps.lessonTitle: Install and Maintain Everyday Apps
steps.title: Update and remove deliberately
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Update RPMs with DNF and user Flatpaks separately. Before removing an app, review dependencies and preserve needed data. Flatpak uninstall without --delete-data normally leaves user app data.
steps.command:
sudo dnf upgrade --refresh
flatpak update --user
flatpak list --user --app
steps.expected: You can explain the two update paths and identify an app’s source.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Check hardware and game support first
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Read the game’s official Linux/Steam requirements. Check GPU support and the current Steam/Proton information. Anti-cheat, DRM and Windows-only launchers may prevent play; some games require Windows.
steps.expected: You selected one compatible test title and recorded the hardware expectation.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Inspect and install Steam from Flathub
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Inspect the exact Steam application ID on Flathub and its permissions. The Flatpak wrapper is community maintained. Review requirements and accept the install only if it fits your system.
steps.command:
flatpak remote-info --user flathub com.valvesoftware.Steam
flatpak install --user flathub com.valvesoftware.Steam
flatpak info --user --show-permissions com.valvesoftware.Steam
steps.expected: Steam is installed in your user Flatpak scope.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Start and sign in
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Launch Steam from Activities or Terminal and let its client updates finish. Sign in privately; never capture the password, QR code or Steam Guard code for evidence.
steps.expected: You reach your own Steam Library.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Try a native title first
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Choose a small Linux-native title that meets the VM or physical machine’s graphics capability. Pick the default library location, inspect required space, and download it. Launch and record the actual result.
steps.expected: The supported test game launches, or you record the specific compatibility failure.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Test Proton separately
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Steam → Settings → Compatibility inspect Steam Play/Proton options. For a compatible Windows title, use its Properties → Compatibility to choose an offered supported Proton version when needed. Test one title at a time.
steps.expected: You can distinguish native Linux execution from a Windows game using Proton.

steps.lessonTitle: Install Steam and Understand Proton
steps.title: Keep libraries and runtimes healthy
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Update user Flatpaks and Steam. Use Steam Settings → Storage to view library usage. For an external library first complete the WD storage class and grant only that path to the Steam sandbox.
steps.expected: You know where the game is stored and how much free space remains.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Inspect network before changing it
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Use Settings → Network or Wi-Fi for your connection. A VMware VM usually sees virtual Ethernet even when Windows uses Wi-Fi. Inspect active connections and addresses.
steps.command:
nmcli connection show --active
ip -br address
ip route
steps.expected: You identify the right adapter and active connection.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Separate DNS from connectivity
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Resolve a known official site, then test HTTPS. If name lookup fails but your network route exists, inspect the connection’s DNS details before changing anything.
steps.command:
getent hosts almalinux.org
curl -I https://almalinux.org
nmcli device show
steps.expected: You can tell a name-resolution error from an HTTPS or connection error.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Add a printer
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open Settings → Printers, unlock if requested, choose Add, and select an allowed detected printer or its confirmed IPP address. Print a single test page.
steps.expected: The queue exists and the actual test page prints.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Configure peripherals
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Settings → Bluetooth pair one device if supported. Test input/output under Sound. In a VM pass through a specific USB device only when needed, then disconnect it when finished.
steps.expected: The chosen device works, or its unsupported state is documented.

steps.lessonTitle: Configure Network, Printing and Sharing
steps.title: Access a known file share
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Files → Other Locations enter the approved smb://server/share address. Use an account authorized for that share and test with a harmless file. Disconnect afterward.
steps.expected: The authorized share opens without changing server permissions.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Identify how the drive reaches AlmaLinux
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: On a physical AlmaLinux PC connect the intended USB drive, or power off and follow the PC manual for an internal SATA installation. In VMware, USB passthrough can attach an external disk exclusively to the guest. For learning, prefer adding a separate NEW virtual disk while powered off. Never use raw access to your Windows system disk.
steps.expected: The drive appears in AlmaLinux without formatting or partition changes.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Match model, serial and capacity
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Open Activities → Disks. Select the candidate drive and record its model, serial, size and partitions. Compare with the physical device label. Inspect terminal output too; do not assume /dev/sdb is always the WD drive.
steps.expected: You positively distinguish the data drive from the system disk mounted at /.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Use an existing data volume without erasing it
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: If it contains files, select its existing partition in Disks and use Mount (play button), or open it from Files. Do NOT choose Format Disk, Format Partition or Delete. Record the actual mount path from Disks and inspect your own files.
steps.expected: Existing files are visible and unchanged.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Prove copy access and available space
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: For a writable mounted volume copy only your harmless notes.txt using Files, reopen it, and compare its SHA-256 with the source. In Terminal quote the ACTUAL mounted path when using df -h or findmnt -T. Do not run a placeholder as a path.
steps.expected: The sample file matches and free space is shown for that mounted filesystem.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Optional: prepare a NEW empty practice disk
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Skip this step for any drive containing data. On a separate disposable blank virtual disk, reconfirm identity in Disks, use its menu → Format Disk → GPT if a partition table is needed, then the + button → Create Partition → choose ext4 for Linux-only practice and a label such as PracticeData. Formatting ERASES selected content; review the device and deletion prompts before confirming.
steps.expected: Only the explicitly empty practice disk has the new Linux filesystem.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Choose persistent mounting only if needed
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Existing removable drives can simply mount from Files when plugged in. For a dedicated Linux data disk, in Disks select the partition → gear → Edit Mount Options; record the existing options, use stable UUID identification, a deliberate path such as /mnt/WDData, and nofail for an optional disk. Test while attached before a reboot. Do not edit the root mount.
steps.expected: The chosen data volume mounts at its intended path and the machine still boots.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Understand what space you added
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: A disk mounted at /mnt/WDData increases storage available at that path; it does not enlarge /. Keep files there intentionally. On a new empty ext4 practice mount only, use Files as an administrator or a reviewed one-directory ownership change for your user; never recursively chown an existing data tree.
steps.expected: You can explain which filesystem gains files and which remains unchanged.

steps.lessonTitle: Add Storage from a Western Digital Drive
steps.title: Use it for games or disconnect it safely
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: For Steam use a Linux-native dedicated library folder on this mounted drive. Grant only that ACTUAL folder to the user Steam Flatpak (via a permissions manager or reviewed flatpak override --user --filesystem=EXACT_PATH com.valvesoftware.Steam), then add the library in Steam Settings → Storage. When done close apps and unmount/eject before unplugging.
steps.expected: The correct library path is visible, or the data volume ejects cleanly.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Choose what matters
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: List Documents, Pictures, project files, browser exports and game saves you need. Include needed hidden app data deliberately. Do not assume an installed app is the same as its documents.
steps.expected: You have a short backup scope and destination.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Make a dated sample backup
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Files create a dated backup folder on your verified external destination. Copy the Everyday folder and practice notes. Wait for completion, then safely unmount the destination.
steps.expected: The copied files exist on a different device.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Prove restore without overwriting
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Reconnect the destination and copy the sample into ~/RestoreTest using Files. Open it and compare hashes for the original and restored file.
steps.command:
sha256sum ~/DesktopPractice/notes.txt
# Also hash your actual restored file path; compare the full values.
steps.expected: Restored content matches and opens.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Schedule a repeatable habit
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Choose a documented backup tool supported by your selected source or a manual schedule. Record retention, encryption/recovery-key location, and last successful restore test. Keep another copy disconnected or offsite.
steps.expected: Your plan says when to back up and how to recover.

steps.lessonTitle: Back Up Your Desktop and Restore a File
steps.title: Keep VM snapshots separate
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Use powered-off VM snapshots for short experiment rollback, and separate backups for valuable data. Review snapshot growth and remove obsolete snapshots using Workstation’s supported manager.
steps.expected: You can explain rollback versus independent file recovery.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: State the problem precisely
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Record what failed, when, the app, the last change, and whether it happens to all users or one. Reproduce using a harmless action and capture the exact error.
steps.expected: You have one testable problem statement.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Check resources
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Inspect space, memory and running processes. In top press q to exit. A full filesystem can break updates and app state.
steps.expected: You can identify the filesystem or process actually consuming resources.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Inspect services and recent errors
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Read failed units and the current boot’s warning/error journal. Journal access can require authorized sudo; inspect before changing a service.
steps.expected: You can relate an error timestamp and service to the symptom.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Inspect one service deliberately
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: For an actual named failed service, use systemctl status SERVICE and journalctl -u SERVICE -b. Replace SERVICE with the real unit from your previous check. Research the specific error before a restart.
steps.expected: You know the failing dependency/configuration or what evidence is missing.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Respect SELinux and firewall boundaries
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Check SELinux state and active firewall policy. If an app is denied, inspect its logs and the official supported labeling/port guidance. Do not disable SELinux or firewalld as the default workaround.
steps.expected: You recorded current protection state without weakening it.

steps.lessonTitle: Troubleshoot Everyday Linux Problems
steps.title: Recover and prove the fix
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Reverse only the identified change, restore an app config backup, or use the VM recovery checkpoint if necessary. Repeat the original test and save before/after evidence.
steps.expected: The original problem is resolved or narrowed with clear next evidence.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Understand where commands execute
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: The hosted website is copy/help mode. GNOME Terminal runs Bash inside your AlmaLinux VM. The local SONIC companion starts PowerShell on Windows; its WSL tab is a separately installed WSL distro, NOT your VMware VM.
steps.expected: You can name the machine each shell controls.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Start SONIC locally on Windows
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In Windows PowerShell clone the repo if needed, select the published curriculum branch, install app dependencies, then start the local server. Use the URL it prints; do not expose it with a public tunnel.
steps.command:
git clone --branch curriculum/alma-desktop-operations https://github.com/CloudSeamTech/RHEL-SONIC.git
cd RHEL-SONIC
npm ci
npm run dev
steps.expected: SONIC opens on localhost, normally port 3000.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Start the companion in a second Windows window
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: From the same repository root in a second PowerShell window install the companion dependencies and start it. Keep this process open. The random pairing token is private and stays on your computer.
steps.command:
npm run companion:install
npm run companion:start
steps.expected: The companion prints a loopback address and pairing token.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Connect and prove a real Windows result
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: At http://localhost:3000/migration#view=terminal select Windows PowerShell. Paste the token into the local-only field and Connect locally. Run Get-Date twice. Compare with your own Windows clock.
steps.expected: Live date/time output appears from your current Windows account.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Optionally enable SSH inside the AlmaLinux guest
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: For VMware access use GNOME Terminal to install/start the SSH server and inspect its address and firewall. If SSH is not already allowed, add the ssh service only to the active connection’s firewall zone after checking it. This opens private-network SSH access; NAT needs no public port-forward. In firewall-config select the active zone and check the ssh service only for that private connection, then make the reviewed change permanent if needed. Alternatively use firewall-cmd --zone=<your-active-zone> --add-service=ssh, replacing the placeholder; repeat with --permanent only after testing.
steps.command:
sudo dnf install openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd
ip -br address
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
steps.expected: sshd is active and you know the guest’s actual NAT address.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Verify host identity and connect from Windows
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: In the guest inspect the ED25519 host-key fingerprint. In Windows PowerShell use ssh your-user@the-actual-guest-IP and compare the offered fingerprint before accepting. The text user/IP are placeholders; substitute your own. Use native PowerShell for a full interactive SSH session; the SONIC panel can relay basic prompts but is not a full-screen terminal emulator.
steps.command:
sudo ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
# Above: AlmaLinux guest only. Then run ssh with your actual user/IP in Windows.
# After SSH connects: whoami; hostname; cat /etc/os-release
steps.expected: You reach the intended AlmaLinux host and can verify its release and username.

steps.lessonTitle: Connect to Real AlmaLinux Terminal Output
steps.title: Use the right terminal and shut down cleanly
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop → Activities → Terminal, unless the step names Windows or VMware Workstation Pro.
steps.action: Run AlmaLinux desktop commands in GNOME Terminal or your verified SSH session. Use exit to leave SSH. In SONIC choose Disconnect and stop the companion process with Ctrl+C when finished. Stop the local dev server separately.
steps.expected: Remote/local prompts are distinguishable and the companion is no longer listening when stopped.
